title: d- and f-block
group: CHEM-ATOM / CHEM-PER — Atoms & the Periodic Table
examples: How do we calculate the magnetic moment from electron configuration?
Can d-block elements show many different oxidation states?
What is the difference between d-block and f-block elements?

explain.say: Today we explore d-block and f-block elements in the periodic table. These groups show interesting chemical behaviours.
D-block elements are the transition metals you find in the middle of the table. They often form coloured compounds.
F-block elements are the inner transition metals, split into two rows. These are the lanthanides and actinides.
These elements commonly show variable oxidation states. This means they can lose different numbers of electrons. For instance, manganese can show states like plus two or plus seven.
The magnetic moment relates to the unpaired electrons in the atoms. More unpaired electrons mean a larger magnetic moment. We use the spin-only formula for calculation.
Consider the ion $\text{Fe}^{2+}$. Its configuration is $[ ext{Ar}] 3d^6$. It has four unpaired electrons. The magnetic moment is calculated using the formula.

faq.q: Why are the d-block elements called transition metals?
faq.a: They are called transition metals because they can change their oxidation states. They also often form coloured compounds.
asks: Do they always change oxidation states?

faq.q: What is the significance of the magnetic moment?
faq.a: The magnetic moment tells us about the number of unpaired electrons in an ion. This is important for understanding chemical bonding.
asks: How do I know if an ion is magnetic?
What does a large magnetic moment mean?

faq.q: Do all elements in the f-block show variable oxidation states?
faq.a: While many show variability, the f-block elements are generally grouped by their unique filling of the f-orbitals. Their chemistry is complex.
asks: How do f-block elements differ from d-block?

faq.q: When calculating the magnetic moment, do we use the total number of electrons?
faq.a: No, you must only count the number of unpaired electrons. The formula uses this count, which we call n.
asks: Should I use the total electron count?
Does the charge affect the calculation?

faq.q: Is the spin-only formula always accurate for these elements?
faq.a: For many common complexes, the spin-only formula provides a very good approximation. However, crystal field effects can sometimes cause deviations.
asks: Is there another formula for magnetism?
When should I not use this formula?

facts: Transition metals (d-block) often exhibit variable oxidation states.
The magnetic moment calculation relies on the number of unpaired electrons, n.
The f-block elements include the lanthanides and actinides.
A zero magnetic moment indicates all electrons are paired.

quiz.say: For an ion with a $d^3$ configuration, how many unpaired electrons are present?
quiz.why: The three electrons will occupy three separate orbitals, resulting in three unpaired electrons.

wrong.0: This is incorrect because the electrons are filling separate orbitals, not pairing up.
wrong.1: This confuses the number of electrons with the number of unpaired electrons.
wrong.3: This is incorrect because the three electrons are not forced into a single orbital.

quiz.say: If an ion has two unpaired electrons, what is its spin-only magnetic moment?
quiz.why: Plugging n=2 into the formula gives the value $\sqrt{2(2+2)} = \sqrt{8} \approx 2.83$.

wrong.0: This incorrectly uses the number of unpaired electrons directly as the magnetic moment.
wrong.1: This might confuse the number of unpaired electrons with the total number of electrons.
wrong.2: This treats the formula as an addition rather than a square root calculation.

quiz.say: Which type of element group is most likely to show the largest range of oxidation states?
quiz.why: D-block elements, like Manganese, are famous for exhibiting a wide variety of stable oxidation states.

wrong.0: Noble gases are chemically inert and do not typically form compounds with variable states.
wrong.2: While they are complex, their variability is often constrained by the filling of the f-orbitals.
wrong.3: Alkali metals are very simple and almost always show a +1 oxidation state.
